title: Globalization: Foundations, Drivers, Theories & Culture
subject: The Contemporary World
description: Steger's triad, Bauman's metaphors (solids, liquids, flows), dimensions & historical roots, drivers, blessing vs. curse debate, World-System & Network theories, cultural globalization, and glocalization.

questions.question: In Manfred Steger's core distinctions, how do 'globalization,' 'globality,' and 'globalism' differ?
options: Globalization is the process (the how); globality is the condition/destination where borders lose traditional significance (the what); globalism is the ideology promoting free-market global integration (the why).
Globalization is a political party; globality is an ocean trade route; globalism is a smartphone brand.
Globalization is fixed barriers; globality is tariff enforcement; globalism is national isolation.
All three terms mean the exact same economic treaty.
questions.answer: Globalization is the process (the how); globality is the condition/destination where borders lose traditional significance (the what); globalism is the ideology promoting free-market global integration (the why).
questions.explanation: Steger's triad separates the ongoing social process (globalization), the resulting social condition (globality), and the market ideology (globalism).

questions.question: Which thinker described globalization as an ongoing, non-static process involving the 'inexorable integration of markets, nation-states, and technologies to an unprecedented degree'?
options: Thomas Friedman
Zygmunt Bauman
Immanuel Wallerstein
Arjun Appadurai
questions.answer: Thomas Friedman
questions.explanation: Thomas Friedman (author of The World Is Flat) emphasized the unprecedented integration of markets, nation-states, and technologies.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'expansion' and 'intensification' of social relations under globalization?
options: Expansion means raising tariffs; intensification means closing borders.
Expansion means reaching new geographic locations and social spheres; intensification means increasing the frequency, speed, and density of interactions.
Expansion applies only to airplanes; intensification applies only to shipping.
Expansion reduces social media; intensification slows mail delivery.
questions.answer: Expansion means reaching new geographic locations and social spheres; intensification means increasing the frequency, speed, and density of interactions.
questions.explanation: Compare sending mail over weeks (earlier era) versus instant global messaging today (intensification).

questions.question: In Zygmunt Bauman's metaphors of globalization, what do 'solids,' 'liquids,' and 'flows' represent respectively?
options: Solids: barriers/borders that hinder movement (tariffs, walls); Liquids: phenomena moving adaptively without fixed boundaries (digital data, capital); Flows: actual cross-border movement of people, tech, goods, and info.
Solids: liquid oceans; Liquids: mountain ranges; Flows: import taxes.
Solids: smartphones; Liquids: newspapers; Flows: customs checkpoints.
Solids: global treaties; Liquids: national passports; Flows: domestic tariffs.
questions.answer: Solids: barriers/borders that hinder movement (tariffs, walls); Liquids: phenomena moving adaptively without fixed boundaries (digital data, capital); Flows: actual cross-border movement of people, tech, goods, and info.
questions.explanation: Bauman's metaphor captures how modern forces melt rigid boundaries ('solids') into rapid, continuous 'liquids' and 'flows.'

questions.question: Which dimension of globalization primarily encompasses multinational corporations (MNCs), free trade, and institutions like the WTO, IMF, and World Bank?
options: Cultural dimension
Economic dimension
Demographic dimension
Environmental dimension
questions.answer: Economic dimension
questions.explanation: The five major dimensions are Economic, Political, Cultural, Demographic/Social, and Environmental.

questions.question: How do narrow and broad definitions of globalization differ?
options: Narrow focuses mainly on economic integration (trade, finance, investments); broad covers economic, political, cultural, social, and environmental dimensions.
Narrow includes pandemics and K-pop; broad excludes trade and MNCs.
Narrow applies only to Asia; broad applies only to Europe.
Narrow defines treaties; broad defines solely domestic farming.
questions.answer: Narrow focuses mainly on economic integration (trade, finance, investments); broad covers economic, political, cultural, social, and environmental dimensions.
questions.explanation: Philippine banana exports to Japan reflect a narrow economic view, whereas COVID-19 responses or global K-drama culture illustrate a broad definition.

questions.question: Which historical trade networks prove that globalization is NOT a purely recent phenomenon invented by the internet?
options: The Silk Road (Mediterranean to East Asia) and the Manila Galleon Trade (1565–1815 linking Asia, the Americas, and Europe)
Only 21st-century fiber-optic cables
SpaceX satellite constellations
Post-2020 video conferencing platforms
questions.answer: The Silk Road (Mediterranean to East Asia) and the Manila Galleon Trade (1565–1815 linking Asia, the Americas, and Europe)
questions.explanation: O'Rourke & Williamson (2000) emphasize globalization has roots across centuries of colonization and transoceanic trade.

questions.question: If cross-border trade has existed for centuries, what makes contemporary globalization uniquely different?
options: Its unprecedented scale, velocity, and geographic range (seen in global supply chains, rapid financial contagion, and fast-spreading disease vectors)
The complete disappearance of national governments
The elimination of all ocean shipping
A total halt in human migration
questions.answer: Its unprecedented scale, velocity, and geographic range (seen in global supply chains, rapid financial contagion, and fast-spreading disease vectors)
questions.explanation: Modern speed and scale mean events like the 2008 financial crisis or COVID-19 reverberate worldwide almost immediately.

questions.question: What are the two main drivers accelerating contemporary globalization according to Part 2 of the Midterm Reviewer?
options: Higher border walls and slower cargo ships
Decline in trade and investment barriers (tariffs/quotas policed by WTO) AND technological change (internet, jet airliners, containerization)
Elimination of all multinational firms and end of telecommunications
Replacement of currency with barter systems
questions.answer: Decline in trade and investment barriers (tariffs/quotas policed by WTO) AND technological change (internet, jet airliners, containerization)
questions.explanation: Lowered policy barriers plus breakthroughs in ICT and transport shrink effective distance across the globe.

questions.question: Which four human feats contribute to the 'Shrinking World' concept?
options: Modern Transportation, Information & Communication Technology (ICT), Medical Advancement, and Technological Innovation
Mercantilism, Isolationism, Censorship, and Deforestation
Feudalism, Tariffs, Quotas, and Border Walls
Monopolies, Sanctions, Strikes, and Embargoes
questions.answer: Modern Transportation, Information & Communication Technology (ICT), Medical Advancement, and Technological Innovation
questions.explanation: These four advancements make distant parts of the planet feel closer and more tightly connected.

questions.question: Which argument supports the 'Blessing' side of globalization?
options: Cultural homogenization eroding native languages
Economic growth, poverty reduction, faster innovation/medical transfer, and wider consumer choice at lower prices (trade grew >50-fold from 1970–2015)
Worker exploitation in unregulated sweatshops
Rapid global spread of financial crises
questions.answer: Economic growth, poverty reduction, faster innovation/medical transfer, and wider consumer choice at lower prices (trade grew >50-fold from 1970–2015)
questions.explanation: Proponents highlight growth, innovation diffusion, cultural exchange, and expanded consumer choice.

questions.question: Which concern belongs to the 'Curse' (critics') arguments against globalization?
options: Widening inequality/worker exploitation, local job displacement, cultural homogenization, environmental degradation, and transnational crisis vulnerability
Lower consumer prices and wider choices
Rapid sharing of life-saving vaccines
Increased transnational cooperation
questions.answer: Widening inequality/worker exploitation, local job displacement, cultural homogenization, environmental degradation, and transnational crisis vulnerability
questions.explanation: Mitigating these curses requires fair labor standards, environmental protections, and safety nets for vulnerable communities.

questions.question: How does Immanuel Wallerstein's World-System Theory view globalization and structure the world economy?
options: As a flat web of equal internet nodes
As a direct product of capitalism's global expansion organized into a three-tier hierarchy: Core, Semi-Periphery, and Periphery
As a purely cultural exchange of food and music
As an alliance of equal cities with no inequality
questions.answer: As a direct product of capitalism's global expansion organized into a three-tier hierarchy: Core, Semi-Periphery, and Periphery
questions.explanation: World-System Theory focuses on unequal structural positions in the global capitalist economy.

questions.question: In World-System Theory, how do wealth and resources flow among the Core, Semi-Periphery, and Periphery?
options: Raw materials and low-cost labor flow upward (Periphery -> Semi-Periphery -> Core), while capital, high technology, and finished goods flow downward
Periphery nations control global finance and set trade rules for the Core
All three tiers retain 100% of their resources with zero trade
Capital flows exclusively from Periphery to Core without finished goods
questions.answer: Raw materials and low-cost labor flow upward (Periphery -> Semi-Periphery -> Core), while capital, high technology, and finished goods flow downward
questions.explanation: Core nations (e.g., US, Western Europe) dominate finance and tech, while Semi-Periphery (e.g., Mexico, Brazil) and Periphery supply manufacturing, raw goods, and labor.

questions.question: What distinguishes Network Theory from World-System Theory?
options: Network Theory views globalization as a rigid pyramid ruled by one state.
Network Theory views globalization as a web of interconnected nodes with multidirectional flows of info, goods, capital, and people—where a change in one node affects all others.
Network Theory denies the existence of the internet.
Network Theory focuses solely on colonial tariffs.
questions.answer: Network Theory views globalization as a web of interconnected nodes with multidirectional flows of info, goods, capital, and people—where a change in one node affects all others.
questions.explanation: Network Theory emphasizes relationships, webs, and interconnections regardless of nation-state hierarchy.

questions.question: According to Jan Nederveen Pieterse (2009), what does cultural globalization typically produce rather than total global uniformity?
options: Cultural diversity and hybrid practices ('global melange' / heterogeneity)
Complete elimination of all music and food
Universal adoption of a single language overnight
Isolation of rural villages from all media
questions.answer: Cultural diversity and hybrid practices ('global melange' / heterogeneity)
questions.explanation: Pieterse argues cross-border cultural exchange creates creative hybrids rather than pure homogenization.

questions.question: What did Arjun Appadurai (1996) observe about cross-border cultural flows, and what did Manuel Castells (2000) call the ICT-driven paradigm?
options: Appadurai: cultural flows enable exchange but can disrupt local traditions; Castells: Informationalism
Appadurai: World-System pyramid; Castells: Solids and liquids
Appadurai: container shipping; Castells: GATT tariffs
Appadurai: Manila Galleon; Castells: Globalism
questions.answer: Appadurai: cultural flows enable exchange but can disrupt local traditions; Castells: Informationalism
questions.explanation: Appadurai studied cross-border cultural scapes/flows, while Castells analyzed the network society powered by Informationalism.

questions.question: Which scenario is the clearest example of 'glocalization'?
options: A Filipino student listening to an unaltered South Korean pop song
McDonald's adding McSpaghetti and rice meals in the Philippines or McAloo Tikki in India
A nation imposing a 100% tariff on all imported cars
Two states signing an environmental treaty
questions.answer: McDonald's adding McSpaghetti and rice meals in the Philippines or McAloo Tikki in India
questions.explanation: Glocalization adapts global brands, ideas, or formats (like local reality TV editions) to fit local tastes and cultures.

questions.question: In the Part 6 Academic Framework, which scholar explains that globalization operates within an 'interstate system' of sovereign yet economically unequal nation-states?
options: Immanuel Wallerstein (2004)
Manuel Castells (2000)
Jan Nederveen Pieterse (2009)
Thomas Friedman (2005)
questions.answer: Immanuel Wallerstein (2004)
questions.explanation: Wallerstein emphasized how powerful economies shape rules within a competitive interstate system.

questions.question: If an international reality TV franchise launches a Philippine edition featuring Filipino hosts, contestants, and cultural humor, this illustrates:
options: Cultural homogenization
Glocalization
World-System periphery extraction
Solidity
questions.answer: Glocalization
questions.explanation: Adapting a global media format to local hosts and cultural context is classic glocalization.

questions.question: A young listener in Brazil streaming South Korean K-Pop or a diner eating Japanese sushi in Paris primarily illustrates:
options: Cultural Globalization
Trade Deficit
Free-Rider Problem
Solidity
questions.answer: Cultural Globalization
questions.explanation: Cultural globalization describes how ideas, foods, music, and values travel across borders.

questions.question: According to the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), what negative flows accompany positive flows like capital, ideas, and goods?
options: Only printed books
Weaponry, viruses/disease vectors, and greenhouse gas emissions
Local handicrafts only
Domestic tax receipts
questions.answer: Weaponry, viruses/disease vectors, and greenhouse gas emissions
questions.explanation: Global flows include both beneficial exchanges and shared transnational threats.

questions.question: What does the characteristic 'Creation of Global Consciousness' refer to?
options: Individuals increasingly seeing themselves as global citizens connected to humanity beyond strict national borders
Forgetting one's own national language
Replacing all local governments with one king
Refusing to follow international news
questions.answer: Individuals increasingly seeing themselves as global citizens connected to humanity beyond strict national borders
questions.explanation: Global flows foster awareness of shared global challenges and responsibilities.

questions.question: When a semiconductor factory flood in one country halts smartphone assembly and delays retail deliveries worldwide, this exemplifies:
options: Stretching of social activities across distant regions
Pure national self-sufficiency
Cultural homogenization
Glocalization
questions.answer: Stretching of social activities across distant regions
questions.explanation: Events and disruptions in one location rapidly impact livelihoods and markets across the globe.

questions.question: Why is 'containerization' in shipping listed as a key technological driver of globalization?
options: Standardized shipping containers drastically lowered transport costs and sped up loading/unloading of global cargo
Containers prevented ships from crossing oceans
Containers are used only for storing digital files
Containers eliminated the need for airplanes
questions.answer: Standardized shipping containers drastically lowered transport costs and sped up loading/unloading of global cargo
questions.explanation: Alongside jet airliners and the internet, containerization made global supply chains economically viable.

questions.question: Within Driver 1 (Decline in Trade and Investment Barriers), what is the primary role of the World Trade Organization (WTO)?
options: To police the global trading system and ensure member nations adhere to agreed trade rules
To manufacture smartphones in Vietnam
To deploy UN peacekeeping troops
To issue global passports
questions.answer: To police the global trading system and ensure member nations adhere to agreed trade rules
questions.explanation: The WTO oversees trade agreements and adjudicates trade barrier disputes among member states.

questions.question: In globalization debates, which view treats globalization as uneven, fragmented, and historically overhyped rather than a uniform transformation?
options: Skepticism
Hyperglobalism
Informationalism
Globalism
questions.answer: Skepticism
questions.explanation: Skeptics contend globalization is piecemeal and fragmented rather than affecting every place uniformly.

questions.question: Migration, rapid urban concentration, and the cross-border mobility of workers belong to which dimension of globalization?
options: Demographic / Social dimension
Environmental dimension
Solidity dimension
Geological dimension
questions.answer: Demographic / Social dimension
questions.explanation: Human mobility, remittances, and global workforce shifts fall under the demographic/social dimension.

questions.question: Why are pollution, deforestation, climate change, and pandemics classified under the Environmental dimension of globalization?
options: Because ecological impacts and pathogens disregard national borders and affect shared global ecosystems
Because trees are sold only in local markets
Because air stays strictly inside one country's territory
Because only rich countries experience weather
questions.answer: Because ecological impacts and pathogens disregard national borders and affect shared global ecosystems
questions.explanation: Environmental risks are inherently transnational and require cooperative solutions.

questions.question: If a researcher asks: 'Which theory explains why wealthy countries capture high-tech profits while poorer nations supply cheap raw materials and labor?'—the best fit is:
options: World-System Theory
Network Theory
Glocalization
Informationalism
questions.answer: World-System Theory
questions.explanation: World-System Theory directly analyzes unequal economic positions between Core, Semi-Periphery, and Periphery.

questions.question: A smartphone designed in the US, using chips from Taiwan, batteries from China, and assembled in Vietnam illustrates:
options: Complex global supply chains and flows across borders
Economic isolationism
Cultural homogeneity
Barter trade
questions.answer: Complex global supply chains and flows across borders
questions.explanation: Appadurai's flows and global production networks coordinate specialized inputs across multiple countries.

questions.question: According to Part 3 of the Midterm Reviewer, how should international bodies respond to the 'Blessing vs. Curse' trade-off?
options: By abolishing all international trade
By promoting sustainable trade, fair labor standards, environmental protections, and policies shielding vulnerable communities from economic shocks
By allowing unregulated exploitation of workers
By eliminating all consumer choices
questions.answer: By promoting sustainable trade, fair labor standards, environmental protections, and policies shielding vulnerable communities from economic shocks
questions.explanation: Thoughtful governance aims to maximize globalization's benefits while mitigating its harms.
